rationale: A wins because it keeps the three real stories separate and refuses to spend facts it does not have. Its line "It is only a story if the company can explain the link between an open release and paid revenue" does actual strategic work; B's "giving the model away to sell everything around it" states the monetization theory before the proof exists. B has usable bones, but A is the set I would let near a reporter list first.
gaps_in_A: "Why a company with $3B in revenue is giving its foundation model away" still assumes open-sourcing equals free distribution; the set asks for license terms, but the headline spends a little proof before collecting it.
"Story type: funding-mechanics" is slightly off. This is a late-stage private-markets disclosure story, not funding unless there is a round, filing, or transaction.
"closed-API vendors are being asked to respond" is a reporting tactic, not a supplied peg. Keep it as outreach logic, not evidence.
gaps_in_B: "giving the model away to sell everything around it" invents monetization the update does not provide; its own proof list admits "what the company actually sells around the model" is missing.
"finance, healthcare, government" are plausible regulated sectors, but they are not in the update. Useful examples, bad facts.

"legally or contractually can't route sensitive data through a closed hosted API" over-specifies the buyer constraint; the update says regulated enterprises, not legal prohibition or hosted-API architecture.
"land grab" and "frontier-quality models" add tech-blog perfume right where the facts are weakest: the update says benchmarks are company-run.
